meaning: A DNA molecule with associated proteins, organized as a distinct genetic unit.
example: A condensed genetic structure becomes visible as a cell prepares to divide.
importantDistinction: An unreplicated chromosome has one DNA molecule; a replicated chromosome has two sister chromatids until they separate.
whatItDoes: A condensed genetic structure becomes visible as a cell prepares to divide.
feature: A condensed genetic structure becomes visible as a cell prepares to divide.
confusion: An unreplicated chromosome has one DNA molecule; a replicated chromosome has two sister chromatids until they separate.

meaning: DNA and its associated proteins in the nucleus, often less condensed between divisions.
example: Genetic material appears less individually distinguishable during much of interphase.
importantDistinction: Chromatin and condensed chromosomes are different organizations of the same genetic material.
whatItDoes: Genetic material appears less individually distinguishable during much of interphase.
feature: Genetic material appears less individually distinguishable during much of interphase.
confusion: Chromatin and condensed chromosomes are different organizations of the same genetic material.

meaning: A pair of chromosomes with the same genes at corresponding loci, one typically inherited from each parent.
example: A maternal and paternal chromosome carry the same gene positions but may carry different alleles.
importantDistinction: Homologues are not the same as two copies made by DNA replication.
whatItDoes: A maternal and paternal chromosome carry the same gene positions but may carry different alleles.
feature: A maternal and paternal chromosome carry the same gene positions but may carry different alleles.
confusion: Homologues are not the same as two copies made by DNA replication.

meaning: One of each type of chromosome characteristic of a species.
example: A human gamete contains one set of 23 chromosomes.
importantDistinction: The number of sets, not the X shape, defines ploidy.
whatItDoes: A human gamete contains one set of 23 chromosomes.
feature: A human gamete contains one set of 23 chromosomes.
confusion: The number of sets, not the X shape, defines ploidy.

meaning: The ordered sequence of growth, DNA replication and division in a dividing cell.
example: A cell grows, copies DNA, prepares for division and then divides.
importantDistinction: Not every cell continuously cycles; some leave the active cycle.
whatItDoes: A cell grows, copies DNA, prepares for division and then divides.
feature: A cell grows, copies DNA, prepares for division and then divides.
confusion: Not every cell continuously cycles; some leave the active cycle.

meaning: The G1, S and G2 parts of the cycle between divisions.
example: A cell carries out metabolism and replicates its DNA before mitosis.
importantDistinction: Interphase is active preparation and function, not a period with no activity.
whatItDoes: A cell carries out metabolism and replicates its DNA before mitosis.
feature: A cell carries out metabolism and replicates its DNA before mitosis.
confusion: Interphase is active preparation and function, not a period with no activity.

meaning: The part of interphase during which DNA is replicated.
example: Each chromosome is copied before its chromatids are separated.
importantDistinction: DNA amount increases without an immediate doubling of chromosome number.
whatItDoes: Each chromosome is copied before its chromatids are separated.
feature: Each chromosome is copied before its chromatids are separated.
confusion: DNA amount increases without an immediate doubling of chromosome number.

meaning: The two replicated copies of a chromosome before their separation.
example: Two copied DNA structures remain associated at the centromere region.
importantDistinction: After separation, each chromatid is counted as an individual chromosome.
whatItDoes: Two copied DNA structures remain associated at the centromere region.
feature: Two copied DNA structures remain associated at the centromere region.
confusion: After separation, each chromatid is counted as an individual chromosome.

meaning: The chromosome region associated with the attachment and separation of sister chromatids.
example: Sister chromatids remain linked at a constricted chromosome region before division.
importantDistinction: Counting separated centromere units helps distinguish chromosomes from chromatids.
whatItDoes: Sister chromatids remain linked at a constricted chromosome region before division.
feature: Sister chromatids remain linked at a constricted chromosome region before division.
confusion: Counting separated centromere units helps distinguish chromosomes from chromatids.

meaning: The count of individual chromosomes in a specified cell or nucleus.
example: A diploid model cell retains four chromosomes after replication until sister chromatids separate.
importantDistinction: Always state which cell, nucleus or pole is being counted.
whatItDoes: A diploid model cell retains four chromosomes after replication until sister chromatids separate.
feature: A diploid model cell retains four chromosomes after replication until sister chromatids separate.
confusion: Always state which cell, nucleus or pole is being counted.

meaning: The quantity of DNA in the specified cell or nucleus.
example: The DNA quantity doubles during S phase before the cell divides.
importantDistinction: DNA amount can change while chromosome number stays the same.
whatItDoes: The DNA quantity doubles during S phase before the cell divides.
feature: The DNA quantity doubles during S phase before the cell divides.
confusion: DNA amount can change while chromosome number stays the same.

meaning: The mitotic stage in which sister chromatids separate and move toward opposite poles.
example: Copied chromosome units become independent chromosomes as they separate.
importantDistinction: The whole-cell chromosome count briefly increases before cytokinesis.
whatItDoes: Copied chromosome units become independent chromosomes as they separate.
feature: Copied chromosome units become independent chromosomes as they separate.
confusion: The whole-cell chromosome count briefly increases before cytokinesis.

meaning: The mitotic stage in which chromosomes condense and the division machinery becomes organized.
example: Condensed replicated chromosomes become visible as spindle structures develop.
importantDistinction: DNA replication precedes prophase in the normal cycle.
whatItDoes: Condensed replicated chromosomes become visible as spindle structures develop.
feature: Condensed replicated chromosomes become visible as spindle structures develop.
confusion: DNA replication precedes prophase in the normal cycle.

meaning: The mitotic stage in which replicated chromosomes align at the cell equator.
example: Replicated chromosomes line up individually across the middle of the cell.
importantDistinction: Homologous pairs do not normally align as tetrads in mitotic metaphase.
whatItDoes: Replicated chromosomes line up individually across the middle of the cell.
feature: Replicated chromosomes line up individually across the middle of the cell.
confusion: Homologous pairs do not normally align as tetrads in mitotic metaphase.

meaning: A microtubule structure involved in chromosome attachment and movement during division.
example: Fibres from opposite poles attach to the replicated chromosome’s kinetochore regions.
importantDistinction: Spindle attachment guides chromosome movement; it does not create new DNA.
whatItDoes: Fibres from opposite poles attach to the replicated chromosome’s kinetochore regions.
feature: Fibres from opposite poles attach to the replicated chromosome’s kinetochore regions.
confusion: Spindle attachment guides chromosome movement; it does not create new DNA.

meaning: The mitotic stage in which chromosome groups reach the poles and daughter nuclei form.
example: Nuclear envelopes reform around the two chromosome groups.
importantDistinction: Cytokinesis is a separate, coordinated division of the cytoplasm.
whatItDoes: Nuclear envelopes reform around the two chromosome groups.
feature: Nuclear envelopes reform around the two chromosome groups.
confusion: Cytokinesis is a separate, coordinated division of the cytoplasm.

meaning: Division of the cytoplasm into separate daughter cells.
example: Two daughter nuclei become enclosed within separate cells.
importantDistinction: Nuclear division and cytoplasmic division are related but not identical.
whatItDoes: Two daughter nuclei become enclosed within separate cells.
feature: Two daughter nuclei become enclosed within separate cells.
confusion: Nuclear division and cytoplasmic division are related but not identical.

meaning: An inward constriction of an animal cell during cytokinesis.
example: A dividing animal cell pinches inward at its middle.
importantDistinction: A rigid plant cell wall prevents this same pinching mechanism.
whatItDoes: A dividing animal cell pinches inward at its middle.
feature: A dividing animal cell pinches inward at its middle.
confusion: A rigid plant cell wall prevents this same pinching mechanism.

meaning: A developing partition that contributes to the new wall between dividing plant cells.
example: Vesicles fuse in the middle of a plant cell to establish a separating partition.
importantDistinction: Plant cytokinesis builds a partition rather than simply pinching a rigid wall inward.
whatItDoes: Vesicles fuse in the middle of a plant cell to establish a separating partition.
feature: Vesicles fuse in the middle of a plant cell to establish a separating partition.
confusion: Plant cytokinesis builds a partition rather than simply pinching a rigid wall inward.

meaning: A control mechanism that helps determine whether a cell proceeds to a later stage.
example: A cell with damaged DNA pauses instead of immediately entering division.
importantDistinction: Checkpoint failure can contribute to uncontrolled division; rapid normal growth is not automatically cancer.
whatItDoes: A cell with damaged DNA pauses instead of immediately entering division.
feature: A cell with damaged DNA pauses instead of immediately entering division.
confusion: Checkpoint failure can contribute to uncontrolled division; rapid normal growth is not automatically cancer.

meaning: The first meiotic division, in which homologous chromosomes separate.
example: Members of each replicated homologous pair move to opposite poles.
importantDistinction: Sister chromatids normally remain together during this division.
whatItDoes: Members of each replicated homologous pair move to opposite poles.
feature: Members of each replicated homologous pair move to opposite poles.
confusion: Sister chromatids normally remain together during this division.

meaning: Pairing of homologous chromosomes during prophase I.
example: Maternal and paternal homologues align closely along corresponding regions.
importantDistinction: This pairing differs from individual chromosome alignment in mitosis.
whatItDoes: Maternal and paternal homologues align closely along corresponding regions.
feature: Maternal and paternal homologues align closely along corresponding regions.
confusion: This pairing differs from individual chromosome alignment in mitosis.

meaning: A paired set of two replicated homologous chromosomes containing four chromatids.
example: Two replicated homologues align as a four-chromatid unit.
importantDistinction: A tetrad contains two chromosomes, not four independently counted chromosomes.
whatItDoes: Two replicated homologues align as a four-chromatid unit.
feature: Two replicated homologues align as a four-chromatid unit.
confusion: A tetrad contains two chromosomes, not four independently counted chromosomes.

meaning: A division that reduces chromosome sets from diploid to haploid, as in meiosis I.
example: One homologue of each pair enters each daughter cell.
importantDistinction: Reduced sets can coexist with chromosomes still having two chromatids.
whatItDoes: One homologue of each pair enters each daughter cell.
feature: One homologue of each pair enters each daughter cell.
confusion: Reduced sets can coexist with chromosomes still having two chromatids.

meaning: The second meiotic division, in which sister chromatids separate.
example: Each of two haploid cells distributes its remaining copied chromosome units.
importantDistinction: No normal S phase occurs between meiosis I and meiosis II.
whatItDoes: Each of two haploid cells distributes its remaining copied chromosome units.
feature: Each of two haploid cells distributes its remaining copied chromosome units.
confusion: No normal S phase occurs between meiosis I and meiosis II.

meaning: The formation and development of gametes.
example: Meiotic products differentiate into functional reproductive cells.
importantDistinction: Meiosis is part of gamete formation, but differentiation and cytoplasm allocation also matter.
whatItDoes: Meiotic products differentiate into functional reproductive cells.
feature: Meiotic products differentiate into functional reproductive cells.
confusion: Meiosis is part of gamete formation, but differentiation and cytoplasm allocation also matter.

meaning: The process producing sperm from precursor cells in the testes.
example: One primary spermatocyte can produce four haploid sperm through division and differentiation.
importantDistinction: Mature sperm form through further differentiation after meiosis.
whatItDoes: One primary spermatocyte can produce four haploid sperm through division and differentiation.
feature: One primary spermatocyte can produce four haploid sperm through division and differentiation.
confusion: Mature sperm form through further differentiation after meiosis.

meaning: A small cell produced during unequal meiotic divisions in oogenesis.
example: Most cytoplasm remains in one developing egg while small cells receive other chromosome sets.
importantDistinction: Polar bodies receive chromosomes but relatively little cytoplasm.
whatItDoes: Most cytoplasm remains in one developing egg while small cells receive other chromosome sets.
feature: Most cytoplasm remains in one developing egg while small cells receive other chromosome sets.
confusion: Polar bodies receive chromosomes but relatively little cytoplasm.

meaning: Exchange of corresponding DNA segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes during prophase I.
example: A chromatid contains segments derived from both parental homologues.
importantDistinction: Crossing over rearranges existing alleles rather than creating every new allele.
whatItDoes: A chromatid contains segments derived from both parental homologues.
feature: A chromatid contains segments derived from both parental homologues.
confusion: Crossing over rearranges existing alleles rather than creating every new allele.

meaning: Independent orientation and segregation of different homologous chromosome pairs during meiosis I.
example: The maternal member of one pair can segregate with either parental member of another pair.
importantDistinction: Genes close together on one chromosome do not necessarily assort independently.
whatItDoes: The maternal member of one pair can segregate with either parental member of another pair.
feature: The maternal member of one pair can segregate with either parental member of another pair.
confusion: Genes close together on one chromosome do not necessarily assort independently.

meaning: Formation of new combinations of existing genetic variants.
example: A gamete carries an allele combination different from the parental chromosome arrangement.
importantDistinction: A new allele combination is not necessarily a new DNA mutation.
whatItDoes: A gamete carries an allele combination different from the parental chromosome arrangement.
feature: A gamete carries an allele combination different from the parental chromosome arrangement.
confusion: A new allele combination is not necessarily a new DNA mutation.

meaning: The chance combination of gametes contributing to a zygote.
example: One of many possible sperm chromosome combinations joins one of many possible egg combinations.
importantDistinction: It adds variation beyond the combinations produced by one meiosis.
whatItDoes: One of many possible sperm chromosome combinations joins one of many possible egg combinations.
feature: One of many possible sperm chromosome combinations joins one of many possible egg combinations.
confusion: It adds variation beyond the combinations produced by one meiosis.

meaning: A body cell other than a gamete or its germ-line precursor context.
example: Skin cells contribute to body tissues rather than fertilizing an egg.
importantDistinction: Many somatic cells use mitosis, but not all divide continuously.
whatItDoes: Skin cells contribute to body tissues rather than fertilizing an egg.
feature: Skin cells contribute to body tissues rather than fertilizing an egg.
confusion: Many somatic cells use mitosis, but not all divide continuously.

meaning: The lineage of cells that gives rise to gametes.
example: Precursor cells in reproductive tissue ultimately contribute genetic information to offspring.
importantDistinction: Germ-line cells are not the same as every supporting cell in a gonad.
whatItDoes: Precursor cells in reproductive tissue ultimately contribute genetic information to offspring.
feature: Precursor cells in reproductive tissue ultimately contribute genetic information to offspring.
confusion: Germ-line cells are not the same as every supporting cell in a gonad.

meaning: Nuclear division that normally preserves chromosome number in daughter nuclei.
example: A diploid precursor produces two nuclei each retaining two chromosome sets.
importantDistinction: Mitosis can also occur in haploid organisms or stages.
whatItDoes: A diploid precursor produces two nuclei each retaining two chromosome sets.
feature: A diploid precursor produces two nuclei each retaining two chromosome sets.
confusion: Mitosis can also occur in haploid organisms or stages.

meaning: A two-division process after one DNA replication that reduces chromosome sets and generates haploid products.
example: A diploid precursor produces haploid nuclear products for a sexual life cycle.
importantDistinction: Meiosis is not simply two independent cycles of mitosis with replication before each.
whatItDoes: A diploid precursor produces haploid nuclear products for a sexual life cycle.
feature: A diploid precursor produces haploid nuclear products for a sexual life cycle.
confusion: Meiosis is not simply two independent cycles of mitosis with replication before each.

meaning: Failure of homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids to separate properly during division.
example: Both members intended for different products move into one product.
importantDistinction: The outcome depends on which division and chromosome are affected.
whatItDoes: Both members intended for different products move into one product.
feature: Both members intended for different products move into one product.
confusion: The outcome depends on which division and chromosome are affected.

meaning: An abnormal number of individual chromosomes rather than complete chromosome sets.
example: A cell has one extra copy of chromosome 21 while most other chromosomes retain their usual copy number.
importantDistinction: Aneuploidy differs from gaining an entire extra set.
whatItDoes: A cell has one extra copy of chromosome 21 while most other chromosomes retain their usual copy number.
feature: A cell has one extra copy of chromosome 21 while most other chromosomes retain their usual copy number.
confusion: Aneuploidy differs from gaining an entire extra set.

meaning: Presence of three copies of one chromosome in an otherwise diploid context.
example: A zygote has three copies of one chromosome type.
importantDistinction: Trisomy is 2n + 1, not three complete sets.
whatItDoes: A zygote has three copies of one chromosome type.
feature: A zygote has three copies of one chromosome type.
confusion: Trisomy is 2n + 1, not three complete sets.

meaning: Presence of only one copy of a chromosome in an otherwise diploid context.
example: A zygote is missing one chromosome from an expected pair.
importantDistinction: Monosomy is 2n − 1, not the loss of every second chromosome.
whatItDoes: A zygote is missing one chromosome from an expected pair.
feature: A zygote is missing one chromosome from an expected pair.
confusion: Monosomy is 2n − 1, not the loss of every second chromosome.

meaning: Production of offspring without fusion of gametes.
example: A new hydra develops from a bud on one parent.
importantDistinction: Asexual offspring can still acquire mutations.
whatItDoes: A new hydra develops from a bud on one parent.
feature: A new hydra develops from a bud on one parent.
confusion: Asexual offspring can still acquire mutations.

meaning: A reproductive process involving combination of gametic genetic contributions.
example: Haploid gametes join to restore a diploid stage.
importantDistinction: Meiosis and fertilization can occur at different positions in different life cycles.
whatItDoes: Haploid gametes join to restore a diploid stage.
feature: Haploid gametes join to restore a diploid stage.
confusion: Meiosis and fertilization can occur at different positions in different life cycles.

meaning: Division of a prokaryotic cell into two cells after its genetic material is copied.
example: A bacterium copies its chromosome and divides.
importantDistinction: Bacteria do not use nuclear mitosis because they do not have a membrane-bound nucleus.
whatItDoes: A bacterium copies its chromosome and divides.
feature: A bacterium copies its chromosome and divides.
confusion: Bacteria do not use nuclear mitosis because they do not have a membrane-bound nucleus.

meaning: Transfer of genetic material between cells through direct contact.
example: A bacterium transfers a plasmid to another cell.
importantDistinction: Transfer can increase genetic variation without directly increasing cell number.
whatItDoes: A bacterium transfers a plasmid to another cell.
feature: A bacterium transfers a plasmid to another cell.
confusion: Transfer can increase genetic variation without directly increasing cell number.

meaning: A plant life cycle with multicellular diploid sporophyte and haploid gametophyte stages.
example: A diploid plant stage produces spores that grow into a haploid stage.
importantDistinction: This is alternation of chromosome-set stages, not merely taking turns between two adult sizes.
whatItDoes: A diploid plant stage produces spores that grow into a haploid stage.
feature: A diploid plant stage produces spores that grow into a haploid stage.
confusion: This is alternation of chromosome-set stages, not merely taking turns between two adult sizes.

meaning: The diploid multicellular generation that produces haploid spores by meiosis.
example: A familiar conifer tree produces spores within reproductive structures.
importantDistinction: A sporophyte makes spores by meiosis, not gametes directly in this model.
whatItDoes: A familiar conifer tree produces spores within reproductive structures.
feature: A familiar conifer tree produces spores within reproductive structures.
confusion: A sporophyte makes spores by meiosis, not gametes directly in this model.

meaning: The haploid multicellular generation that produces gametes by mitosis.
example: A haploid plant stage produces eggs or sperm without another ploidy reduction.
importantDistinction: A haploid stage can produce gametes by mitosis.
whatItDoes: A haploid plant stage produces eggs or sperm without another ploidy reduction.
feature: A haploid plant stage produces eggs or sperm without another ploidy reduction.
confusion: A haploid stage can produce gametes by mitosis.

meaning: A reproductive cell that can develop without fusing with another cell.
example: A haploid product of plant meiosis grows into a gametophyte.
importantDistinction: A spore differs from a gamete, which participates in fusion.
whatItDoes: A haploid product of plant meiosis grows into a gametophyte.
feature: A haploid product of plant meiosis grows into a gametophyte.
confusion: A spore differs from a gamete, which participates in fusion.
